contentProvenance.instrumentLabels: IPIP official Johnson (2014) key; original labels retained
contentProvenance.descriptiveText: Trajectas preparation draft authored 2026-10-29 from the facet constructs and item content. Not a published interpretive manual, a validated competency mapping, a set of normative bands or a clinical interpretation.
contentProvenance.midIndicatorPolicy: Middle descriptions are contextual prompts, not classifications as population average.
contentProvenance.factorPolicy: The library importer copies each construct to one composition-locked factor; do not create additional factor rows.

domains.name: Neuroticism
domains.definition: Typical frequency and intensity of distress, emotional reactivity and difficulty coping with pressure.
low: Usually remains emotionally steady.
Experiences fewer worries or frustrations.
Recovers composure relatively readily.
high: Experiences distress or worry more readily.
domains.context: Lower reactivity can support steadiness; greater sensitivity may bring concerns to attention. Neither end establishes coping skill, mental health status or leadership effectiveness.
domains.reflection: Identify situations that intensify emotional reactions and the responses that help you act constructively.

domains.name: Extraversion
domains.definition: Typical engagement with social interaction, assertive action, activity, excitement and positive emotion.
low: Often prefers quieter or more solitary settings.
May allow others to initiate interaction.
Can favour a measured pace and lower stimulation.
high: Often seeks social engagement and stimulation.
Is more inclined to speak up or take the lead.
Can prefer a busy and energetic pace.
domains.context: A quieter approach can suit independent concentration; an outgoing approach can suit frequent interaction. Effectiveness depends on the situation and behaviour.
domains.reflection: Consider when to initiate and speak up, and when to listen, slow down or allow space for others.

domains.name: Openness to Experience
domains.definition: Interest in imagination, aesthetics, feelings, unfamiliar experiences, abstract ideas and reconsidering conventional values.
low: Often favours familiar and concrete approaches.
May prefer established routines or views.
Can place less emphasis on abstract or aesthetic exploration.
high: Often explores ideas, imagination and unfamiliar experiences.
May attend closely to feelings or aesthetics.
Can be more willing to question conventional views.
domains.context: Familiar approaches can support continuity; exploration can support discovering alternatives. This domain is not a test of intelligence, creativity performance or adaptability skill.
domains.reflection: Choose where exploration could add value and where an established approach should be retained or tested carefully.

domains.name: Agreeableness
domains.definition: Typical interpersonal trust, candour, helpfulness, cooperation, modesty and concern for others.
low: May be more sceptical or guarded with others.
Can place personal interests or direct challenge first.
May take a more self-promoting or emotionally detached approach.
high: Often gives others the benefit of the doubt.
Is more inclined to help, cooperate and show concern.
May take a modest and accommodating approach.
domains.context: A challenging approach can surface disagreement; a cooperative approach can support relationships. Context determines whether trust, accommodation or challenge is appropriate.
domains.reflection: Consider how to balance care and cooperation with clear boundaries, candid disagreement and appropriate scrutiny.

domains.name: Conscientiousness
domains.definition: Typical perceived effectiveness, orderliness, commitment, achievement striving, self-discipline and deliberation.
low: May prefer a less structured or more spontaneous approach.
Can be less focused on commitments, targets or sustained task effort.
May decide with less advance deliberation.
high: Often organises work and takes commitments seriously.
Is inclined to pursue goals and persist with tasks.
domains.context: Structure and persistence can support follow-through; a less structured style may allow spontaneity. Neither end establishes competence or actual delivery.
domains.reflection: Review whether planning, effort and checking match the task, and where flexibility or a clearer commitment would help.

facets.name: Anxiety
facets.definition: Proneness to worry, fear and anticipatory tension.
low: Usually worries less.
Feels less threatened by uncertain outcomes.
Reports fewer fears.
high: Often anticipates what could go wrong.
facets.context: Lower anxiety may make uncertainty easier to tolerate; greater concern can prompt preparation. Neither end establishes risk judgement.
facets.reflection: Distinguish useful preparation from repetitive worry and identify a practical next action.

facets.name: Anger
facets.definition: Readiness to experience irritation, frustration and anger.
low: Is usually difficult to irritate.
Reports less frequent anger.
Often tolerates frustrations calmly.
high: Can react strongly to perceived provocation.
facets.context: Lower anger can support calm exchanges; anger can signal that a boundary or concern needs attention. The expression and consequences of anger require separate evidence.
facets.reflection: Notice early signs of irritation and choose how to express a concern without escalating the exchange.

facets.name: Depression
facets.definition: Tendency to experience low mood, discouragement and negative feelings about oneself, as represented by these personality items.
low: Reports fewer periods of feeling down.
Usually feels more comfortable with oneself.
Is less prone to discouragement.
high: More often feels down or discouraged.
facets.context: This is a personality facet score, not a diagnosis or a measure of clinical severity. Interpret experiences in context rather than labelling capability.
facets.reflection: Reflect on situations associated with discouragement and the support, routines or adjustments that are helpful.

facets.name: Self-Consciousness
facets.definition: Discomfort with social attention, approaching others or potentially embarrassing situations.
low: Is less troubled by social attention.
Approaches unfamiliar people more readily.
Feels less constrained by possible embarrassment.
high: Feels less comfortable in unfamiliar social situations.
facets.context: Lower discomfort can make public participation easier; greater sensitivity may encourage preparation. This facet does not measure self-awareness or insight.
facets.reflection: Identify a manageable way to participate in situations where attention or unfamiliarity feels uncomfortable.

facets.name: Immoderation
facets.definition: Difficulty resisting cravings, temptations and urges to overindulge.
low: Finds temptations easier to resist.
Usually regulates indulgence.
Reports more control over cravings.
high: Finds strong cravings harder to resist.
facets.context: The content concerns regulation of appetites and indulgence. It should not be treated as a comprehensive measure of impulsive decision-making.
facets.reflection: Identify tempting situations and decide in advance what limits or routines would be useful.

facets.name: Vulnerability
facets.definition: Tendency to feel overwhelmed or unable to cope when facing stress or difficult events.
low: Usually feels able to cope under pressure.
Maintains composure during difficult events.
Is less readily overwhelmed.
high: Can feel unable to deal with demands.
facets.context: Lower vulnerability reflects reported steadiness under stress; it does not demonstrate coping skill or recovery from adversity. Greater vulnerability can highlight situations that need support.
facets.reflection: Identify demands that become overwhelming and the practical supports or actions that help restore control.

facets.name: Friendliness
facets.definition: Warmth and ease in approaching and engaging with other people.
low: Maintains more interpersonal distance.
May be slow to approach new people.
Can prefer a more reserved manner.
facets.context: A reserved approach can preserve boundaries; warmth can make contact easier. Relationship effectiveness still depends on behaviour and context.
facets.reflection: Choose when to initiate contact and when to respect personal or professional distance.

facets.name: Gregariousness
facets.definition: Preference for company, crowds and frequent social interaction rather than solitude.
low: Often prefers solitude or smaller settings.
May avoid crowds.
Needs less frequent social contact.
high: Is comfortable with crowded social settings.
facets.context: Solitude can support concentration and recovery; company can provide stimulation and connection. Neither preference establishes teamwork skill.
facets.reflection: Plan a workable balance between social contact and quieter time.

facets.name: Assertiveness
facets.definition: Inclination to take charge, express direction and assume a leading role.
low: Often lets others lead.
May be less inclined to take control.
Can prefer a less directive role.
high: Often seeks control of group action.
facets.context: Taking charge can help a group act; allowing others to lead can support participation. More assertiveness does not automatically produce more effective leadership.
facets.reflection: Consider when clear direction is needed and when to invite input or share control.

facets.name: Activity Level
facets.definition: Preference for a busy, active and fast-moving pace of life.
low: Often prefers a leisurely pace.
Allows more downtime.
May avoid keeping continuously busy.
facets.context: A measured pace can allow reflection and recovery; activity can support engagement with a busy environment. This facet does not establish productivity.
facets.reflection: Check whether your pace matches the task and whether adequate recovery or momentum is needed.

facets.name: Excitement-Seeking
facets.definition: Appetite for excitement, adventure and stimulating or potentially reckless experiences.
low: Prefers lower stimulation.
May avoid adventurous situations.
Usually has less appetite for excitement.
high: May be attracted to reckless experiences.
facets.context: Lower stimulation can suit predictable settings; excitement can make stimulating settings appealing. This facet does not establish the quality of risk decisions.
facets.reflection: Distinguish the appeal of excitement from the benefits and consequences of a particular action.

facets.name: Cheerfulness
facets.definition: Frequency and expression of positive emotion, enjoyment and enthusiasm.
low: Expresses less visible joy.
May experience positive emotion less frequently.
Can take a more subdued emotional tone.
high: Can take an enthusiastic or positive tone.
facets.context: A subdued style need not indicate distress; cheerfulness can make positive engagement visible. Neither end alone establishes realism or performance.
facets.reflection: Consider how your emotional expression affects others and when a realistic concern should also be voiced.

facets.name: Imagination
facets.definition: Interest in fantasy, daydreaming and a vivid inner imaginative life.
low: Focuses more on concrete experience.
Spends less time daydreaming.
May have less interest in fantasy.
high: Can become absorbed in fantasy or thought.
facets.context: Concrete attention can support practical focus; imagination can provide possibilities. This facet is not a test of creative problem-solving performance.
facets.reflection: Choose when imaginative exploration is useful and how to connect possibilities with practical action.

facets.name: Artistic Interests
facets.definition: Interest in art, poetry, beauty and aesthetic experience.
low: Has less interest in artistic activities.
May give aesthetics less attention.
Often prefers other forms of engagement.
high: May enjoy art, poetry or museums.
facets.context: Different levels of artistic interest reflect preferences rather than artistic skill or leadership capability.
facets.reflection: Consider whether aesthetic experiences add enjoyment or perspective without treating them as a performance requirement.

facets.name: Emotionality
facets.definition: Attention to, intensity of and interest in emotional experience.
low: Pays less attention to emotional reactions.
May experience feelings less intensely.
Can find emotional expression harder to relate to.
facets.context: Lower emotional emphasis can support emotional distance; stronger emotional experience can bring feelings into awareness. This facet does not establish emotion-reading accuracy or emotional intelligence.
facets.reflection: Notice relevant feelings while checking interpretations of other people's emotions through conversation.

facets.name: Adventurousness
facets.definition: Preference for variety and unfamiliar experiences rather than familiar routines and conventional ways.
low: Often favours familiar approaches.
Prefers established routines.
May dislike changes to known ways.
high: Is more open to unfamiliar experiences.
May be less attached to conventional routines.
facets.context: Familiarity can support continuity; variety can support exploration. Preference for change is different from effective adaptation to change.
facets.reflection: Decide where trying something unfamiliar is worthwhile and what preparation or continuity is needed.

facets.name: Intellect
facets.definition: Interest in abstract ideas, challenging material and theoretical or philosophical discussion.
low: Often prefers concrete or practical material.
Has less interest in theoretical discussion.
May find abstract ideas less appealing.
high: Often engages with theory or philosophy.
facets.context: Concrete and abstract interests can each suit different work. This is a self-report personality facet, not an intelligence or reasoning test.
facets.reflection: Match the level of abstraction to the problem and seek evidence that ideas can explain or improve something useful.

facets.name: Liberalism
facets.definition: Willingness to question conventional social values, as operationalised here using political and moral-attitude items.
low: More often endorses conventional or conservative views.
May favour established social rules.
Can prefer firmer moral boundaries.
high: More often endorses liberal political views.
Can be more willing to reconsider conventions.
facets.context: The original English items concern political and moral attitudes. This facet does not establish leadership quality, fairness, learning agility or organisational suitability.
facets.reflection: Discuss the meaning of differing views without treating a political preference as a capability score.

facets.name: Trust
facets.definition: Readiness to believe that other people are honest, well-intentioned and dependable.
low: Is more sceptical of others' intentions.
May verify claims before relying on them.
Can be guarded in extending trust.
high: Gives others the benefit of the doubt.
facets.context: Scrutiny can protect against misplaced trust; trust can make cooperation easier. The appropriate balance depends on evidence and consequences.
facets.reflection: Choose how much trust to extend and what verification is proportionate to the situation.

facets.name: Morality
facets.definition: Reported avoidance of manipulating, cheating, exploiting or obstructing other people.
low: May endorse more instrumental treatment of others.
Can be more willing to gain advantage at others' expense.
May report obstructive or exploitative behaviour.
high: Is less inclined to manipulate others for gain.
Usually rejects obstructing others for personal advantage.
facets.context: The retained scale label is Morality. These self-reports are not verification of integrity, ethical conduct or honesty-humility.
facets.reflection: Examine concrete decisions and their effects on other people rather than treating the label as a character verdict.

facets.name: Altruism
facets.definition: Inclination to care about other people's needs and offer practical help.
low: May give others' needs less attention.
Is less inclined to spend time helping.
Can prefer clearer boundaries around assistance.
high: Is willing to spend time supporting people.
facets.context: Boundaries can protect capacity; helping can support others. Effective support requires attention to what help is needed and what is sustainable.
facets.reflection: Balance useful assistance with clear priorities, consent and sustainable boundaries.

facets.name: Cooperation
facets.definition: Inclination to avoid interpersonal aggression, retaliation and unnecessary conflict.
low: May be more confrontational.
Can respond to conflict with hostility.
May be inclined to retaliate.
high: Is less inclined to insult or retaliate.
facets.context: A cooperative approach can reduce friction. Constructive disagreement and assertive boundaries should be distinguished from the aggression represented by the lower end.
facets.reflection: Raise disagreements directly while avoiding insults, revenge or unnecessary escalation.

facets.name: Modesty
facets.definition: Restraint in claiming superiority, praising oneself or drawing attention to one's virtues.
low: Readily expresses a high opinion of oneself.
May emphasise personal virtues.
Can make superiority claims.
facets.context: Visible self-advocacy can communicate achievements; modesty can leave room for others. This facet does not establish accurate self-insight or confidence.
facets.reflection: Describe achievements with evidence while recognising the contributions and strengths of others.

facets.name: Sympathy
facets.definition: Compassion and concern for people experiencing hardship or disadvantage.
low: Maintains more distance from others' difficulties.
May give hardship less attention.
Can prefer to avoid distressing concerns.
high: Feels concern for people facing hardship.
facets.context: Emotional distance can help maintain boundaries; compassion can draw attention to unmet needs. Neither alone establishes sound decisions or effective assistance.
facets.reflection: Consider others' needs alongside evidence, fairness and the practical consequences of a response.

facets.name: Self-Efficacy
facets.definition: Belief in one's effectiveness at completing tasks and handling practical demands.
low: Reports less confidence in task effectiveness.
May doubt how well tasks will be handled.
Can feel less certain about getting things done.
high: Usually expects to know how to get things done.
facets.context: Confidence can support willingness to act; doubt can encourage checking or assistance. This facet measures perceived effectiveness rather than demonstrated competence.
facets.reflection: Compare confidence with task evidence and identify where practice, feedback or help would improve calibration.

facets.name: Orderliness
facets.definition: Preference for tidiness, organisation and returning belongings to their proper place.
low: Is less concerned with tidiness.
May leave belongings out of place.
Can prefer a less orderly environment.
facets.context: An orderly environment can make retrieval and routines easier; less concern with tidiness may suit some flexible settings. This facet does not establish planning or management skill.
facets.reflection: Use enough structure to make work manageable without adding organisation that serves little purpose.

facets.name: Dutifulness
facets.definition: Reported commitment to promises, truthfulness and following rules.
low: May treat commitments or rules more flexibly.
Can report breaking promises.
May be less consistent about truthfulness.
facets.context: Commitment can support reliability. Whether a rule should be followed or challenged requires judgement beyond this self-report facet.
facets.reflection: Make commitments explicitly, raise difficulties early and explain any necessary challenge to an inappropriate rule.

facets.name: Achievement-Striving
facets.definition: Willingness to work hard, exceed requirements and invest effort in achievement.
low: May be satisfied with meeting minimum requirements.
Often invests less additional effort.
Can place less emphasis on demanding achievement.
facets.context: A measured level of striving can protect other priorities; strong striving can sustain demanding goals. Actual outcomes and the value of the goals require separate evidence.
facets.reflection: Choose goals deliberately and check that effort remains proportionate to priorities and available capacity.

facets.name: Self-Discipline
facets.definition: Inclination to start tasks, stay prepared and carry plans through rather than delay or waste time.
low: May delay starting tasks.
Can find follow-through difficult.
May spend time on competing distractions.
facets.context: Sustained task focus can support completion; willingness to pause can sometimes allow reprioritisation. The facet does not establish whether a task should be continued.
facets.reflection: Identify the next useful action and review whether persistence or a deliberate change of plan is needed.

facets.name: Cautiousness
facets.definition: Tendency to deliberate before acting rather than rush into decisions.
low: May act quickly with limited advance thought.
Can make spontaneous decisions.
May rush into action.
high: Is less inclined to make rash decisions.
facets.context: Speed can matter when action is urgent; deliberation can help examine consequences. Neither end establishes decision quality or an appropriate appetite for risk.
facets.reflection: Match the amount of deliberation to the stakes, time available and reversibility of the decision.
